newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries steady in London as tone improves.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries steady in London as tone improves.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries prices were little changed in London on Thursday, but analysts said there was a better tone of the market.

So far in the session interest in Treasuries has been overshadowed by European data, but attention will switch to the U.S. with international trade data and the Philadelphia Fed survey due later, they said.
"It has been very quiet and most of the focus has really been in Europe rather than the U.S.," said a treasuries trader at a U.S. bank in London. "We are pretty close to where we went out yesterday."
"There has been a two-way flow with slightly better selling in twos and threes," he said.
At 1005 GMT, the long bond was at 94-06 to yield 7.10 percent, versus 94-08 in Tokyo and 94-05 at the New York close.

Two-year T-notes were at 99-20, yielding 6.46 percent, unchanged from both Tokyo and New York. The benchmark three-year note was at 98-04 to yield 6.61 percent, compared with 98-04 in Tokyo and 98-03 in New York.
February international trade data are due at 1230 GMT. A Reuters consensus of economists expectations is forecasting a deficit of $10.1 billion compared with a $12.71 billion deficit in January.

Adam Chester, international bond strategist at Yamaichi International in London said the trade balance had reached a record defict in January and February's figure was expected to show a modest improvement.
"But in terms of levels it still represents a fairly strong number," he said. "Today's figures are not expected to be particularly market friendly."
Also due is one of the first sets of numbers for April, the Philadelphia Fed survey, to be released at 1400 GMT. Forecasts are for the survey to be at 20.4, versus 21.1 in March.

"It is the first insight into what manufacturing conditions were like going into the second quarter," said Chester. "And all the indications are that the manufacturing activity has remained fairly strong."
Chester said the market's resilience had been impressive when it bounced sharply after strong industrial production data on Wednesday.

Treasuries had been helped by comments from Federal Reserve vice chair Alice Rivlin that she had voted for a rate increase in March but was not sure whether further rate rises were needed to cool the economy, he said.

"Generally, there is a slightly better feel to the market now suggesting we might have found a low," Chester said. He said Thursday's data was not as important for the market as Wednesday's numbers and given the improved tone he expected any dips to be bought.
June T-bond futures were at 107-20 in automated trade, up 5/32 from Wednesday's Chicago settlement.
